text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Sweden will be able to retain its strict laws on the import of alcohol and tobacco for some years, it emerged from the first round of negotiations with other European Union countries. Most members are ready to accede to Swedish demands for exemptions until June, 2000.

- An investigation into the murder of Olof Palme must start again from the beginning, 10 years after the statesman was shot dead in a Stockholm street, a meeting of police officers and prosecutors decided. Theories of a conspiracy will be treated as seriously as the belief that the Social Democratic politician was killed by a single gunman.

- The chairman of Sweden's metalworkers' union, Goran Johnsson, said that trade unions would have to raise their demands in forthcoming wage collective bargaining unless politicians "ceased dabbling in higher energy taxes and insurance contributions."
- The market for personal computers in Sweden is slowing, leaving small and large firms looking for partners or other ways to increase their market share.

- Much of Swedish parliament favours cutting employer fees in certain sectors as opposed to across the board as a means to create new jobs. The service sector, for example, is being considered for such cuts.
